div.p: This paper presents a new aperiodic request server in real-time energy harvesting system. This server handles hard periodic tasks and soft aperiodic tasks, using ED-H in order to schedule periodic tasks. The main principle of the server is to minimize response times of aperiodic tasks without compromising the schedulability of periodic tasks. The server, known as SSP (Slack stealing with Energy Preserving), enhances the response time offered by the Slack stealing approach, because of idle times and energy surplus. Finally, performance evaluation is made by comparing the server with two background servers.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: In real-time energy harvesting system, the limited amount of energy stored in the batteries exhausts the lifetime of battery-powered systems. Replacing battery in some wireless network applications is either impractical or expensive, because using the battery as the only energy source balks the perpetual performance of such applications. Consequently, the benefit of supplying these devices with energy harvesting has great potential to permit systems to achieve energy autonomy and to maintain energy efficiency. Energy harvesting is the process by which energy is derived from external sources such as sunlight, thermal, etc. and it is converted into electrical energy for further use. Several technical challenges were described to divulge the vantage of energy harvesting systems [7].

In fact, a real-time energy harvesting system demands that its results be logically correct and delivered on time without causing energy shortage. In this paper, we expose the problem of scheduling hard periodic task (task with regular arrival time and deadline) and also soft aperiodic tasks (task with no deadline, no regular arrival time) under energy constraints. Thus, the main scheduling problem objective when dealing with this kind of tasks depending on their arrival pattern, is to guarantee that all hard tasks will be executed by Earliest Deadline with energy Harvesting (ED-H) rules [5] while providing good response time for aperiodic tasks. ED-H is proved optimal in [5] in the sense that any task set scheduled by any algorithm on a given energy constrained platform can be executed by ED-H. It relies on avoiding any future potential failure. In brief, the concept of our proposed algorithm is to schedule soft aperiodic tasks as soon as possible without compromising the timing and energy constraints on periodic tasks.

This paper is constructed as follows. Related work is shown in Section II. Model and terminology are explained in Section III. Background materials are presented in Section IV. Scheduling of aperiodic tasks is discussed in section V and section VI respectively. Finally, the conclusion is given in section VIII.

div.head: Related Work
div.p: Many server mechanisms have been investigated on the scheduling of periodic tasks and soft aperiodic tasks. In literature, this problem have been considered in static priority as well as in dynamic priority environments. Spuri and Buttazzo propose the Total Bandwidth (TB) server to enhance aperiodic responsiveness [10]. As the name of the server indicates, the total bandwidth of the server is immediately assigned to the aperiodic task upon its arrival to the system, and then it is scheduled by the EDF algorithm, as any other periodic task.

Chetto and Chetto used the optimal "Slack Stealer" service to propose the so-called Earliest Deadline as Late as possible (EDL) server [4] [9] [11]. Stealing all the possible processing time from the periodic tasks to service the aperiodic tasks earlier, consists the basic idea of Slack Stealing [12] [13].

These algorithms provide a useful framework to guarantee and execute tasks with hard time and no energy constraints. Our work targets to present an optimal algorithm that solves the problem of jointly scheduling both periodic and aperiodic tasks in an energy harvesting environment [14]. Our proposal "Slack Stealer with energy Preserving " SSP server balance performance and implementation overhead. It is a variation of the EDL server while considering energy consumption by tasks and harvested power from the environmental energy source.

div.head: Model and Terminology
div.p: 3.0.1. Task Model. We study the case of a Hard Real-Time Energy Harvesting system which is composed of periodic and soft aperiodic tasks constrained with energy. A periodic task set is denoted as follows:
div.formula: τ = {τ i | 1 ≤ i ≤ n}. A four-tuple (C i , D i , T i , E i ) is associated with each τ i .
div.p: In this characterization, τ i makes its first request at time 0 and its subsequent requests at times kT i , k = 1, 2, ... called release times. H is the least common multiple of the request periods T i , called the hyper-period. Each request has a Worst Case Execution Time (WCET) of C i time units, an absolute deadline D i , a period T i and a Worst Case Energy Consumption (WCEC) of E i energy units. It is not necessary that E i be proportional to C i . The processor utilization of the periodic task set τ is U pp = τi τ Ci Ti which is less than or equal to 1. The energy utilization of τ is defined as
div.formula: U ep = τi τ Ei Ti .
div.p: A job is any request that a task makes. A four-tuple (r j , C j , E j , d j ) is associated to a job J j and gives its release time, WCET, WCEC and (absolute) deadline, respectively. The task set τ gives rise to an infinite set of jobs which are scheduled by the optimal monoprocessor scheduler ED-H. We assume that the processor sustains only one operating frequency and consumes negligible energy in the idle state when there are no jobs to execute.

In addition, we consider Ap the stream of m soft aperiodic requests, defined as Ap = {Ap i | 1 ≤ i ≤ m} and Ap i = (a i , c i , e i ). a i is the arrival time of a soft aperiodic task, c i is the worst case execution time and e i is the worst case energy requirement. The finish time of Ap i will be denoted by f i .
3.0.2. Energy Model. Our system uses an ideal energy storage unit that has a nominal capacity C of units of energy. The energy level at time t is denoted E(t).
We represent the energy source by P p (t), the instantaneous charging rate produced by the power including all losses. The energy produced by the source on
div.formula: [t 1 , t 2 ) is given as E p (t 1 , t 2 ) = t2 t1 P p (t)dt.
div.p: It is uncontrollable and can be accurately predicted for near future for trivial time and energy cost. We assume that the energy produced in any unit of time can overlap with the energy consumed in one unit of time and that the storage unit is completely charged initially (i.e. E(0) = C). The reserved energy does not leak any energy over time and may be used at any time later [5] [6].

div.head: ED-H scheduling
div.p: The ED-H [5] is a recent scheduling algorithm; which is an extension of EDF, and proved to be optimal for real time tasks scheduling. ED-H enjoins the jobs to execute according to the earliest deadline first rule, after checking that the residual energy capacity of the battery is sufficient to guarantee the energy-feasibility of all future occurring jobs, i.e. execute the active job during at least one time unit must not lead to an energy shortage either for itself or for a future occurring job.

This can be verified by considering the time and energy characteristics of jobs as well as the charging level of the storage unit. If one of the previous conditions is not satisfied, the processor makes its decisions to be idle so that the energy storage unit recharges sufficiently. We may choose to stop the recharge only when the reservoir is filled or the system has no more slack time.
Fundamental scheduling concepts required in the energy harvesting system are: slack time and slack energy.
1) The slack time at time t gives the available processor time after executing uncompleted jobs with deadlines at or before d i . It is given by:
div.formula: ST Ji (t) = d i -t -h(t, d i )(1)
div.p: where h(t, d i ) is the total processing demand of uncompleted jobs at t with deadline at or before d i . By definition, the slack time of a periodic task set τ at current time t as follows:
div.formula: ST τ (t) = min di>t ST Ji (t)(2)
div.p: The slack time represents the maximum continuous time of processor that could be existing at time t while still meeting the deadlines of all the tasks. It is computed using EDL algorithm [4] and will be used to recharge the battery.

2) The Slack Energy at time t is the maximum quantity of energy that can be used on the time interval [t,d i ) while guaranteeing enough energy for jobs released at or after t and deadline at or before d i . The slack energy of J i at current time t by equation 3.
div.formula: SE Ji (t) = E(t) + E p (t, d i ) -g(t, d i )(3)
div.p: where g(t, d i ) represents the total energy required by jobs on the time interval [t, d i ). It is worth noting that if there exists some job J i such that SE Ji (t) = 0, executing any other job with a deadline higher than d i within [t, d i ) will involve energy starvation for J i .
Thus, the slack energy of the periodic task set τ at current time t represents the maximum energy surplus that the system could consume instantaneously at t. The slack energy at t is
div.formula: SE τ (t) = min t<di SE Ji (t)(4)
div.p: 3) The preemption slack energy at the current time t gives the maximum energy that could be consumed by the active job whilst guaranteeing absence of energy starvation for jobs that may preempt it. Let d be the deadline of this active job. The preemption slack energy at t is
div.formula: P SE(t) = min t<di<d SE Ji (t)(5)

div.head: Aperiodic task scheduling
div.p: The Background scheduling is a simple method [8] that treats aperiodic tasks as lowest-priority tasks than periodic tasks. Aperiodic tasks are thus treated in the idle time of the processor. If there are several pending aperiodic tasks, they are served using the FIFO technique (First-In First-Out) which is also known as FCFS (First-Come First-Serve). As the server will have no impact on the sequence, the algorithm ensures the execution of periodic tasks with respect of their time constraints. However, the response time of aperiodic tasks can be very large particularly when the load periodic tasks becomes large.

The Earliest Deadline as Late as possible (EDL) server is based on the Slack Stealing strategy, which ensures aperiodic tasks running within a real-time application. It consists of executing the periodic tasks at the earliest when there is no aperiodic activity. Otherwise, whenever an aperiodic job arrives, all periodic tasks are scheduled at the latest, in compliance with all the deadlines of the tasks. In other words, the EDL algorithm takes advantage of the actual slack (i.e. the interval between the execution end and the due date) of the periodic tasks in order to minimize the time. In [4], Chetto and Chetto present a simple method for determining the localization and duration of idle times in any window of a sequence produced by EDL. EDL has been shown to be optimal, as it minimizes the aperiodic response times of aperiodic tasks among all other algorithms [4].

div.head: Background-based ED-H scheduling:
div.p: In this section, we focus on scheduling tasks based on background policy. In this sense, we present two algorithms: Background with Energy Surplus (BES) and Background with Energy Preserving (BEP). The intuition behind the BES server is to run aperiodic tasks in the absence of periodic tasks and when the replenishment rate of the reservoir is equal to C energy units. Periodic tasks are scheduled according to the ED-H rules.

The BEP server is the second aperiodic server background-based, which is also adapted to run under the optimal algorithm ED-H. Executing the aperiodic tasks as long as this does not involve energy shortage for all future occurring periodic tasks, exposes the main difference that improves the performance of BEP over BES.

div.p: Ap 1 is completely finished at t = 20, where E(20) = 1 energy unit. Its response time is 12 time units. Periodic task set Γ is scheduled according to ED-H till t = 22, where Ap 2 is serviced till t = 23 since there is no waiting periodic task, the reservoir is not empty and SE(t = 22) = 7 > 0. div.head: Slack Stealing-based ED-H scheduling:
div.p: The proposed SSP algorithm is a strategy based on the EDL algorithm with ED-H [14]. It uses the slack time to perform the aperiodic tasks as close as possible and the slack energy to perform the future periodic tasks without causing a shortage of energy. If no aperiodic task occurs, the periodic tasks are scheduled according to ED-H. And if an aperiodic task arrives, it uses the excess energy and non-activity of the processor to serve the aperiodic tasks. If the energy reservoir is not empty and the system has both a slack time and a slack energy, the aperiodic task is served according to FIFO as long as the list of aperiodic tasks is non empty.
The procedure of generating the SSP schedule is summarized in the following Algorithm: Algorithm 1 SSP Require:
t: current time L(t): list of periodic tasks at t Ap(t): list of aperiodic tasks at t 1: while TRUE do if Ap(t) not empty AND reservoir not empty AND SlackEnergy(t) > 0 AND SlackT ime(t) > 0 then

The property of optimality of SSP is attained if the actual execution time of aperiodic requests is equal to the worst execution time. In that, SSP minimizes the response times of aperiodic requests. Theorem 6.1. [14] All periodic tasks meet their deadlines when scheduled according to ED-H with the slack stealer for aperiodic servicing.

Theorem 6.2. [14] For any periodic task set scheduled according to ED-H and a stream of aperiodic tasks processed in FIFO order, the slack stealing algorithm minimizes the response time of every aperiodic task, amongst all algorithms which are guaranteed to meet all deadlines.

div.head: Performance Evaluation
div.p: In this section, we summarize the experimental results compare the performance of SSP algorithm to that of the BEP and BES algorithms by comparing the average response times of soft aperiodic tasks. In all simulations, a set of 30 periodic tasks with periods, durations and energy requirements randomly generated were chosen. Periods and computation times are distributed uniformly in discrete time steps, depending on U p . Energy consumption of every task is proportional to its period and depends on the setting of U e . Periodic task sets are considered to be schedulable in terms of processing time and energy.

The aperiodic load was varied across the margin of processor utilization unused by periodic tasks. Execution times and energy consumption of aperiodic requests are uniformly distributed according to desired values for U ps and U es by modeling a poisson aperiodic arrival. The aperiodic load is denoted by U ps .

Throughout our simulation results, we assume that a total energy load U e includes 50% of the periodic energy utilization U ep and 50% of the aperiodic energy load U es . The interarrival times are chosen so that the aperiodic task arrived and executed before the end of the hyperperiod H, which are predefined at the start of each experiment.

In all experiments, each point in the plots corresponds to the mean response time normalized with respect to the average aperiodic execution time. The average is computed over 100 runs, in which a total of 15000 aperiodic jobs are generated. In this way, a value of 3 on the y-axis means an average response time 3 times longer than the task computation time. The lower the response time curve lies on these graphs, the better the algorithm is for improving aperiodic responsiveness. We assume that the storage capacity is initially full and for simplicity, the recharging power P p is constant as we didn't study, throughout the paper, the impact of power on the algorithms.

For the first experiment (Figure 4, U pp = 0.3 and U e /P p = 0.2), the SSP server provides nearly maximum aperiodic responsiveness up to a total load of 80%. It also provides a significant reduction in average response time compared to BES and BEP (at least 20% lower). In the second experiment (Figure 5, U pp = 0.3 and U e /P p = 0.8), the SSP always provides the best response time performance still with a highly energy constrained system. It takes advantage of the energy slack stealing to outperform the two background servers.

For the third experiment illustrated in Figure 6, the aperiodic load was held constant at 30% and the the system is assumed highly energy constrained U pp = 0.7. We note that the performance benefit of the SSP server over the BEP and BES servers is wider with the increase of the total energy load. The SSP server provides a response time at least 25% lower compared to background servers for all energy load parameters.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: This paper describes a new optimal server for improving the response time for aperiodic tasks in a dynamic realtime energy constrained environment, where periodic tasks are scheduled according to the ED-H algorithm. The SSP server profits from energy surplus as well as processing time surplus to execute aperiodic tasks earlier. Based on this principle, the SSP was proven to be optimal in the sense that it reduces the response time of each aperiodic task. The simulation results show that the SSP behaves better than the two background strategies BEP and BES in all time and energy conditions. In the context of complex computer systems, it reveals a high computational complexity because of the dynamic computation of available slack energy and slack time when necessary.
